findings.issue_text: pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go:611 — [P2, confidence 100] `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` — SQLite cleanup with a large configured batch recopies the entire accumulated ID list on every iteration, producing quadratic allocation and CPU work (IDs 1 through 32767 alone generate 3.44 GB of intermediate strings for a 218 KB query) before issuing a single deletion.

pkg/services/cleanup/cleanup.go:77 — [P2, confidence 100] `ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` — A cleanup pass taking between one and nine minutes now leaves a pending ticker event and immediately starts another pass on completion, continuously running all eight cleanup jobs against the database and filesystem instead of retaining the previous ten-minute cadence; rebuttal: more frequent annotation cleanup reduces the backlog; survives because: the shared timer also accelerates seven unrelated jobs and eliminates their idle interval precisely when cleanup is already expensive, so restoring the multiplier to 10 removes this global workload amplification independently of the annotation batching fix.

pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/cleanup_test.go:132 — [P2, confidence 100] affectedAnnotations, affectedAnnotationTags, err := cleaner.Run(context.Background(), test.cfg) — Every cleanup test completes its inserts before starting cleanup, so the MySQL concurrent-insert deadlock that motivates the SQL rewrite has no regression coverage and remains unverified by the supplied static-only evidence; rebuttal: the sequential integration cases verify retention and the large SQLite batch; survives because: neither exercises concurrent MySQL inserts, the precise condition the new implementation claims to fix.

pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go:615 — [P2, confidence 75] `placeholders := "?" + strings.Repeat(",?", len(ids)-1)` — On PostgreSQL, configuring AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above 65535 and fetching at least 65536 eligible annotations or orphaned tags produces a DELETE exceeding PostgreSQL's [65535 query-parameter limit](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/limits.html), so cleanup returns an error without deleting that batch on every run, whereas the previous subquery DELETE had no bound parameters.

pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go:615 — [P2, confidence 75] `placeholders := "?" + strings.Repeat(",?", len(ids)-1)` — On PostgreSQL, a configured batch size of 65,536 or higher with at least 65,536 eligible rows creates more bind parameters than PostgreSQL's 65,535 limit, so cleanup fails on the same batch every cycle and removes no rows from it; rebuttal: ordinary installations use smaller batches and SQLite already has special handling; survives because: this introduces a PostgreSQL limit absent from the former parameter-free subquery, and neither this branch nor the repository constructor caps or splits the supplied batch ([PostgreSQL limits](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/limits.html)).

pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go:611 — [P2, confidence 100] `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` — For a SQLite batch containing IDs 1 through 32,767, repeatedly copying the accumulated string constructs 3,444,494,248 bytes of intermediate string contents to produce a 218,261-byte ID list, imposing quadratic allocation and garbage-collection work on every such cleanup batch; rebuttal: the batch size bounds memory and this branch avoids SQLite's parameter limit; survives because: SQLite operators using the explicitly supported large batch size incur more than 3 GB of string allocation per batch, and a single strings.Builder or join avoids that cost while preserving the same SQL.

pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go:576 — [P2, confidence 100] `r.log.Error("Tags to clean", "count", len(ids), "ids", ids, "cond", cond, "err", err)` — Every successful orphan-tag cleanup invocation, including an empty database, emits this error-level entry and the subsequent `cleaned tags` error entry with nil errors, so operators monitoring error logs receive false failure signals every cleanup cycle; rebuttal: these messages provide useful cleanup diagnostics; survives because: successful progress is emitted unconditionally at error severity in all three cleanup paths, making error-level monitoring report routine success as a failure.

pkg/services/cleanup/cleanup.go:77 — [P2, confidence 100] `ticker := time.NewTicker(time.Minute * 1)` — On instances whose cleanup cycle finishes within one minute, this changes every cleanup job from six to sixty executions per hour, multiplying unrelated snapshot, dashboard-version, invitation, short-URL, query-history, and temporary-file cleanup work tenfold while the annotation SQL optimization leaves those jobs untouched; rebuttal: a shorter interval reduces annotation backlog after the new two-step deletion; survives because: this shared ticker also accelerates seven unrelated jobs and imposes their additional database and filesystem work on operators without any requirement or optimization for those jobs.

goldens.comment: The code uses Error log level for what appears to be debugging information. This will pollute error logs in production. Consider using Debug or Info level instead.

The cleanup job ticker was changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute, which can lead to increased database load and contention due to more frequent execution of cleanup tasks. This change should be reviewed to ensure it aligns with performance expectations.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go:611 — [P2, confidence 100] `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` — SQLite cleanup with a large configured batch recopies the entire accumulated ID list on every iteration, producing quadratic allocation and CPU work (IDs 1 through 32767 alone generate 3.44 GB of intermediate strings for a 218 KB query) before issuing a single deletion.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a performance bug in the new code at lines 589-592. The code builds a string of IDs using repeated fmt.Sprintf concatenation: `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)`. This pattern creates a new string on each iteration, copying all previous content plus the new ID. For large batch sizes (up to 32767 as shown in the test case), this results in O(n²) string allocations and copies. While the code is functionally correct, this is a real performance defect that could cause significant memory pressure and CPU usage during cleanup operations with large batches on SQLite.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies that the test changes don't include any concurrent insert tests that would verify the MySQL deadlock fix mentioned in the code comments. The diff shows new comments in xorm_store.go stating 'Single-statement approaches, specifically ones using batched sub-queries, seem to deadlock with concurrent inserts on MySQL' and 'We have a bounded batch size, so work around this by first loading the IDs into memory and allowing any locks to flush inside each batch.' However, the test changes only add sequential integration tests - they create annotations, then run cleanup, without any concurrent operations. This is a legitimate concern about missing test coverage for the specific concurrent MySQL deadlock scenario that motivated the implementation change.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go:615 — [P2, confidence 75] `placeholders := "?" + strings.Repeat(",?", len(ids)-1)` — On PostgreSQL, configuring AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize above 65535 and fetching at least 65536 eligible annotations or orphaned tags produces a DELETE exceeding PostgreSQL's [65535 query-parameter limit](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/limits.html), so cleanup returns an error without deleting that batch on every run, whereas the previous subquery DELETE had no bound parameters.

adjudication.rationale: The diff shows that for non-SQLite databases (including PostgreSQL), the code uses parameterized queries with `placeholders := "?" + strings.Repeat(",?", len(ids)-1)` where `ids` can be up to `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` in length. The SQLite case has special handling for batch sizes > 999, but PostgreSQL has a 65535 parameter limit that is not handled. If `AnnotationCleanupJobBatchSize` is configured above 65535 and that many IDs are fetched, the DELETE query would exceed PostgreSQL's parameter limit. The previous subquery-based DELETE didn't have this issue as it used no bound parameters. This is a real defect introduced by the refactoring.

adjudication_records.issue_text: pkg/services/annotations/annotationsimpl/xorm_store.go:611 — [P2, confidence 100] `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` — For a SQLite batch containing IDs 1 through 32,767, repeatedly copying the accumulated string constructs 3,444,494,248 bytes of intermediate string contents to produce a 218,261-byte ID list, imposing quadratic allocation and garbage-collection work on every such cleanup batch; rebuttal: the batch size bounds memory and this branch avoids SQLite's parameter limit; survives because: SQLite operators using the explicitly supported large batch size incur more than 3 GB of string allocation per batch, and a single strings.Builder or join avoids that cost while preserving the same SQL.

adjudication.rationale: The finding correctly identifies a performance issue in the new code at lines 589-593. The diff shows `values = fmt.Sprintf("%s, %d", values, v)` being used in a loop to build a string of IDs. This is indeed a quadratic string concatenation pattern - each iteration creates a new string by copying the entire previous string plus the new value. With the test case showing batch sizes up to 32,767 (annotationCleanupJobBatchSize: 32767), this would cause significant memory churn. The finding's math about 3GB of intermediate allocations is plausible for 32K iterations of growing string copies. Using strings.Builder or strings.Join would be O(n) instead of O(n²). This is a legitimate performance concern for code explicitly designed to handle large batches, though it's not a correctness bug.

adjudication.rationale: The diff clearly shows the ticker interval being changed from 10 minutes to 1 minute in cleanup.go line 77. This ticker controls the Run() method's cleanup cycle which, based on the code structure, would affect all cleanup jobs managed by CleanUpService, not just annotations. The finding correctly identifies that this 10x increase in frequency would affect unrelated cleanup operations (snapshots, dashboard versions, invitations, etc.) that weren't optimized by this PR.
